section.title: Formalising the Notion of a Decision Method
section.para: The Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence identifies three equivalent descriptions of the same notion of constructive witness:

listitem.para: Logic (Curry-Howard). A proof of a proposition P is a term of type P in a typed lambda calculus.
Type theory. A program inhabiting a type A → B is a constructive function mapping evidence of A to evidence of B.
Category theory (Lambek). A morphism in a cartesian closed category corresponds to a proof in intuitionistic propositional logic and to a typed program.

section.para: The dual — the non-correspondence — is equally precise: a sentence for which no proof term, no inhabiting program, and no morphism exists is not constructively witnessed. This gives formal content to Tarski's phrase devices available in T: a device is exactly a constructive witness in the sense of the correspondence.

definition.title: Decider
definition.para: A decider for T is a total Turing machine M that halts on every input φ and accepts if and only if φ ∈ Th(T). The existence of a decider is equivalent to Th(T) being a recursive set.

definition.title: Semi-decider
definition.para: A semi-decider for T is a Turing machine M that accepts every φ ∈ Th(T) and either rejects or diverges on every φ ∉ Th(T). The existence of a semi-decider is equivalent to Th(T) being recursively enumerable (RE).

section.para: Semi-decidability is strictly weaker than decidability: every recursive set is RE, but the converse fails. The set of first-order validities is RE — systematic proof search is guaranteed to halt on every valid sentence by the completeness theorem (Gödel, 1930) — but it is not recursive, as established by Church and Turing (1936).

A classically inconsistent theory T has Th(T) equal to the set of all sentences in its language: every sentence is provable by the principle of explosion. The constant-YES function is then a decider, making every classically inconsistent theory trivially decidable. This conclusion holds regardless of the logical framework used to formalise T, provided that framework validates explosion.
